comment: The pointer half of Aerie's secret handling (the cluster plan Phase 2, docs/secrets-architecture.md).
This file names every secret the cluster needs and where its value comes from at seed time.
It holds NO secret bytes and never will - see docs/ethos.md. It is structural: identical for
every installation, which is exactly why it is committed.
Consumed by scripts/secrets/Sync-AerieSecrets.ps1 (writes the values into the parameter store)
and, from Phase 3 on, by the ExternalSecret manifests under deploy/ that read them back out.
Both halves must agree on these paths, so change them here and nowhere else.
Fields:
key          - path under 'prefix'. Convention: <component>/<key>, lowercase kebab-case.
'component' is the cluster consumer (a Helm release or operator), not the
producer, so a rotation is scoped by who breaks when it's wrong.
env          - environment variable Sync-AerieSecrets.ps1 reads the value from. Deliberately
not always equal to the GitHub name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID would be picked
up by the AWS CLI itself and silently seed with the wrong identity.
githubSource - the repository secret or variable provision-2-seed-secrets.yml maps into 'env'.
Where the value lives *today*; nothing downstream of the seed depends on it.
githubKind   - which tab of Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions holds it. An AWS access
key *id* is an identifier, not credential material, so it is a 'variable': it
stays unmasked in run logs, where seeing which identity a run used is most of
troubleshooting a permissions failure. Every value that is actually secret -
secret access keys, tokens, passwords - is a 'secret'. Getting this wrong is
silent: ${{ secrets.X }} for a value stored as a variable resolves to empty.
required     - a run fails preflight if a required value is missing, and skips an optional one.
phase        - the the cluster plan phase that first consumes it. Optional entries ahead of their
phase are listed so the convention is settled before the manifest needs it.
kubernetes   - the Kubernetes Secret this parameter lands in, and therefore the ExternalSecret
that syncs it. Its presence is what makes a manifest exist under
deploy/cluster/infrastructure/config/external-secrets/ - generated from this
file by New-ExternalSecrets.ps1 and checked by ci.yml, never hand-written.
Fields: 'namespace', 'secretName', 'secretKey' (the key inside that Secret),
'consumedBy' (prose, reproduced as a comment in the generated manifest),
'dockerconfigjson' (optional - the registry host; renders a
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret via ESO's target.template instead of a
plain Opaque one, for a pull secret rather than a value a Deployment reads as
an env var). This may be a single block or an array of blocks, for a value that
lands in more than one namespace (a pull secret both the kubelet and
image-reflector-controller need) - every parameter naming the same namespace
and secretName, across every block, becomes ONE ExternalSecret with one key per
parameter, which is how a credential pair stays a single object that cannot
half-rotate. Only a 'required: true' parameter may carry this: an ExternalSecret
pointing at a parameter no run ever seeded sits in SecretSyncError indefinitely
and takes its Kustomization's Ready condition - and with it the phase gate -
down with it.
kubernetesDeferred - the other half of that rule: why a required parameter has no manifest
yet, naming the phase that adds one. Every required entry carries exactly one
of these two fields, so a value can be seeded and then quietly never consumed
only on purpose, in writing.
The one imperative secret injection the design allows (docs/ethos.md): the credential the
cluster uses to reach its own secret store. Everything else above is declarative from here on.
This is the 'aerie-eso' IAM user - read-only on the tree above, separate from both the
seed writer and 'aerie-restic'. ESO's ClusterSecretStore in Phase 3 references this Secret.

'aerie' rather than a namespace of its own because 8b.10 repoints deploy/cluster/data/schema/restore-job.yaml at this same Secret and deletes the hand-made aerie-pg-restore-restic - one object serves the side that writes backups and the side that reads them, and the CronJob needs this namespace anyway to reach aerie-pg-app.

parameters.description: restic repository password. Seeded here for the Phase 8 CronJob; the printed offline copy remains the root of trust and this parameter never replaces it.

parameters.description: aerie-restic IAM user, scoped to the backup bucket only.

kubernetes.consumedBy: 8b.5 backup CronJob, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY; the restore Job reads it from here too after 8b.10

parameters.description: Secret half of the aerie-restic credential.

kubernetes.consumedBy: 8b.9 backupTargetCredentialSecret. The key name is Longhorn's, not this file's convention: it reads the Secret by these literal names and reports an unusable backup target rather than an error if they differ. AWS_ENDPOINTS is the third name Longhorn documents and is deliberately absent - it exists for non-AWS S3, and an empty value is not the same as an omitted one.

parameters.description: aerie-longhorn IAM user (8a.1), scoped to the Longhorn backup bucket alone - its own identity for the same reason aerie-restic and aerie-eso are separate. Its Secret's keys are SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE against every other entry in this file and have to be: Longhorn reads backupTargetCredentialSecret by the literal names AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and reports an unusable backup target rather than an error if they are anything else. env is deliberately not AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID - the AWS CLI would pick that name up on the seeding runner, the same collision the Route53 and CNPG pairs are renamed around.
Secret half of the aerie-longhorn credential. Minted by hand (8a.1): Set-AerieBackupAws.ps1 creates the user and its policy, but minting an access key means printing one.
CloudNativePG WAL archiving and base backups to S3. Its own IAM user, same isolation discipline as aerie-restic.
Secret half of the CNPG WAL archiving credential.

Region of the WAL bucket. barman-cloud's s3Credentials.region is a SecretKeySelector, not a string, so this has to arrive as a Secret key rather than as a postBuild substitution even though it isn't secret. env is deliberately not AWS_REGION - the AWS CLI would pick that name up directly, which is the same reason the Route53 pair is renamed.
Wi-Fi password embedded in the kiosk Device Owner provisioning QR. Lives in SiteSettings (obfuscated at rest) today; optional here until that moves out of the database.

Tailscale auth key for the subnet router, which runs directly on each Hyper-V host (provision-0-new-node.yml) rather than in the cluster - a subnet router advertising the LAN belongs on a machine with the LAN interface. Not phase-gated: this value never becomes a kubernetes block. See docs/plans/swarm/phase-5-app-tier.md 5b.13.

GitHub username for the fine-grained PAT scoped to the private per-installation site repo (5a.3).
Fine-grained PAT, contents:write on the site repo (5a.3) alone. Flux uses it to commit image-automation's tag bumps.
SMB share username. `guest` if the share keeps today's anonymous access, or a dedicated account (5a.4) - either way required, so the value is never sometimes-seeded.
SMB share password. Empty string for the guest path (5a.4).

kubernetes.consumedBy: docs/plans/deploy-observability.md 1.1 - the grafana-github-datasource plugin, reached as the GITHUB_DATASOURCE_TOKEN env var that 6b.5's grafana.envValueFrom binds and the provisioned datasource reads through Grafana's own __env interpolation

parameters.description: Fine-grained PAT scoped to this repository alone, actions:read + contents:read and nothing else. Read-only and cluster -> GitHub: it grants nothing inbound. 'env' is deliberately not GITHUB_READ_TOKEN - GitHub refuses to store a repository secret whose name starts with GITHUB_, the same collision the Route53 pair is renamed around.

kubernetes.consumedBy: docs/plans/deploy-observability.md 1.3 - notification-controller Provider type 'grafana', secretRef; the key must be named 'token' or the provider falls back to basic auth and 401s

parameters.description: Grafana service-account token with the Editor role, which is the least that can POST /api/annotations. Unlike every other parameter here there is no issuer to fetch it from and no CLI that mints it: it is created once from Grafana's own UI (Administration > Users and access > Service accounts) at the metrics hostname. Rotating it is creating a second token, re-running Provision 2, then deleting the first.

Schwab Trader API OAuth client id - the value the developer portal at developer.schwab.com labels 'App Key'. Named here by docs/plans/trading.md Phase 0b, ahead of the value existing, so that seeding it after the app is approved is a paste rather than a decision. 'phase' is deliberately absent: the consumer is that plan's Phase 2, not a cluster plan phase, and a bare number here would read as the latter. 'required: false' until then - a Sync-AerieSecrets.ps1 run before approval reports 'skipped (no value)' instead of failing preflight over a credential Schwab has not issued yet - and no 'kubernetes' block, because an ExternalSecret for a parameter no run has seeded sits in SecretSyncError indefinitely. Trading Phase 2 flips required to true and adds the block, in the same commit as the code that reads it. 'secret' rather than 'variable' despite being an identifier, which is a deliberate departure from the access-key-id precedent above: that rule is justified by seeing which of several identities a run used, and there is exactly one Schwab app, so the troubleshooting value is nil while an app key in an unmasked run log is a third party able to burn this app's rate limit.

Secret half of the Schwab Trader API OAuth client credential, labelled 'Secret' in the developer portal. Issued with the client id and rotated with it - a pair, which is why trading Phase 2 lands both in one Kubernetes Secret rather than two. Optional and manifest-less for now, same reasoning as its other half.
